mcqs.question: In a UML sequence diagram, what does the vertical dashed line beneath an object's box represent?
options: The object's lifeline — its existence over time
A synchronous message being sent
An activation bar showing active processing
A return value coming back from a prior call
mcqs.explanation: The dashed vertical line is the lifeline, representing the object existing across the diagram's time span. Messages are horizontal arrows, an activation bar is a thin rectangle drawn on top of the lifeline during active work, and return values are dashed horizontal arrows — none of those are the vertical line itself.

mcqs.question: Which arrow style should you use for a call that fires off a background email job without the caller waiting on it?
options: Synchronous — solid line, filled arrowhead
Return message — dashed line, open arrowhead
Asynchronous — solid line, open arrowhead
There's no special notation for this — use a synchronous arrow
mcqs.explanation: A fire-and-forget call that doesn't block the caller is the definition of an asynchronous message, drawn with an open arrowhead. Synchronous implies the caller waits; a return message shows a reply from an already-completed call, which doesn't apply to a job that hasn't finished yet.

mcqs.question: You need to show that checking inventory leads to either a 'proceed' or an 'out of stock' branch. Which diagram type fits better?
options: A sequence diagram, since branching is a kind of message
A class diagram, since inventory is a class
Neither — branching logic can't be represented in UML
An activity diagram, since it structurally represents decisions and branches
mcqs.explanation: Activity diagrams use decision diamonds specifically for branching logic. A sequence diagram would have to bury the branch in a note rather than show it structurally, a class diagram has no notion of flow at all, and UML does have a dedicated notation for this — the decision diamond.

mcqs.question: When whiteboarding a new design from scratch, which diagram should you draw first, and why?
options: The sequence diagram, because it shows what actually happens
The class diagram, because you need the objects defined before you can sequence messages between them
Whichever one the interviewer happens to sketch as an example
Neither — go straight into writing code
mcqs.explanation: You can't draw lifelines and messages for objects that don't exist yet, so the class diagram — establishing the pieces — comes first. A sequence diagram only makes sense once there's structure to sequence interactions between.

mcqs.question: Your sequence diagram for "place an order" has grown to 12 lifelines, including every internal getter call. What should you do?
options: Trim it to the 3-5 objects and calls that cross a real system boundary, relevant to the question asked
Add more detail so the interviewer sees the full depth of your understanding
Switch to a class diagram instead, since it's less detailed by default
Keep it as-is — more lifelines always signals more rigor
mcqs.explanation: Extra lifelines for internal getters cost interview time without adding insight — trimming to the objects and cross-boundary calls that matter to the question is the fix. Piling on more detail or swapping diagram types doesn't address the actual problem, which is scope, not diagram choice.
